## Declarations and implementations

```plato
//==
// # Quantities
//
// Sections, in order:
//  - Quantities — obligation fills for the concrete quantity types
//  - Quantities - per-type Amount / FromAmount projections

library Quantities
{
    //==
    // # Quantities — obligation fills for the concrete quantity types
    //
    // `interface IQuantity` (`quantities.concepts.plato`) inherits `IComparable`, `IHashable`,
    // `IAdditive`, `IScalable`, and `IInterpolatable`. None of those has a generic
    // implementation that a concrete quantity type can inherit for free, so every
    // one of the ~49 physical quantity types owes ten members. Left unfilled, the
    // compiler emits a throwing stub for each — 490 `NotImplementedException`s.
    // The pattern is to write every obligation out per type when no generic shortcut
    // exists.
    //
    // This library takes the same idea one level higher. `IQuantity` declares two
    // members that together make a quantity isomorphic to a `Number`:
    //
    //     Amount(x: Self): Number;          // project to the raw amount
    //     FromAmount(_: Self, x: Number);   // rebuild from a raw amount
    //
    // `FromAmount` is what turns the ten obligations
    // into ten *generic* one-liners over `IQuantity` (below) plus two mechanical
    // per-type lines. Cost falls from 49x10 hand-written bodies to 49x2, and every
    // quantity type gets identical, correct arithmetic instead of 49 chances to
    // mistype a unit conversion.
    //
    // `IQuantity` is one-dimensional and has no intrinsic operator surface
    // to collide with generic fills. `Angle` is the one quantity with intrinsic operators
    // (`intrinsics.library.plato`: Add/Subtract/Multiply/Divide/Negative/Compare/Hash); the
    // intrinsic declarations win for those, and the generics fill only what is left
    // (Lerp, LessThanOrEquals, Modulo, Amount, FromAmount).
    //
    // Naming note: the dispatch-on-ignored-receiver form `FromAmount(_: Self, x)`
    // is the tree's idiom for a constructor-shaped function (compare `Number.Pi` in
    // `constants.library.plato`); zero-argument functions are not idiomatic here.
    //
    // This lives in its own file rather than in `numeric-structures.library.plato`
    // (the P3 package that owns the `IQuantity` *interface*) on purpose. P3 holds
    // derived helpers that are generic over interfaces; what follows is 98 bodies
    // naming 49 concrete types one at a time, which would swamp that file and has a
    // different reason to change — it grows whenever a `quantities-*.plato` file adds
    // a type, not when an interface gains a member. `LIBRARIES.md` ground rule 1 names
    // files `<domain>.library.plato` after the domain they serve;
    // `quantities.library.plato` serving the quantities domain follows that rule
    // directly.

    //==
    // # Generic obligations
    //
    // Ten members, written once against the interface, discharging the
    // IAdditive / IHashable / IOrderable / IInterpolatable / IScalable obligations
    // for every implementing type. Each routes through Amount/FromAmount, so a
    // new quantity type needs only the two projections in the sections below.

    // The sum of two quantities of the same kind.
    Add(a: IQuantity, b: IQuantity): IQuantity
        => a.FromAmount(a.Amount + b.Amount);

    // The difference of two quantities of the same kind.
    Subtract(a: IQuantity, b: IQuantity): IQuantity
        => a.FromAmount(a.Amount - b.Amount);

    // The additive inverse: the same magnitude with the opposite sign.
    Negative(x: IQuantity): IQuantity
        => x.FromAmount(-x.Amount);

    // The additive identity: none of this quantity's unit. The receiver only
    // selects the type. (Zero lives on IAdditive, not INumericalLimits, which
    // quantities do not inherit.)
    Zero(x: IQuantity): IQuantity
        => x.FromAmount(0.0);

    // A digest of the underlying amount, consistent with equality.
    Hash(x: IQuantity): Integer
        => x.Amount.Hash;

    // Total order by amount. Only meaningful between quantities of one kind.
    LessThanOrEquals(a: IQuantity, b: IQuantity): Boolean
        => a.Amount <= b.Amount;

    // Linear interpolation by amount; t is unclamped, so it extrapolates.
    Lerp(a: IQuantity, b: IQuantity, t: Number): IQuantity
        => a.FromAmount(a.Amount.Lerp(b.Amount, t));

    // Scaled by a unitless factor; the unit is unchanged.
    Multiply(x: IQuantity, scalar: Number): IQuantity
        => x.FromAmount(x.Amount * scalar);

    // Divided by a unitless factor; the unit is unchanged.
    // Precondition: scalar is non-zero.
    Divide(x: IQuantity, scalar: Number): IQuantity
        => x.FromAmount(x.Amount / scalar);

    // The remainder after dividing the amount by a unitless factor. Useful for
    // wrapping a quantity into a repeating range.
    Modulo(x: IQuantity, scalar: Number): IQuantity
        => x.FromAmount(x.Amount.Modulo(scalar));

    //==
    // # Quantities - per-type Amount / FromAmount projections
    //
    // The mechanical half of the pattern documented above:
    // two lines per concrete quantity type, naming its canonical-unit field and
    // rebuilding a value from a raw amount in that same unit. Split out of that
    // file because it has a different reason to change - it grows whenever a
    // `quantities-*.plato` file adds a type, not when an interface gains a member.

    //==
    // # Per-type projections
    //
    // Two lines per concrete type: read the canonical-unit field, and rebuild
    // from a raw amount in that same unit. The unit named here is the one in
    // the type's field name, so no conversion happens anywhere in this section.
    // Adding a quantity type to `quantities.types.plato` means adding a pair here.

    //==
    // # Geometric and kinematic quantities

    // Angle <-> a raw amount in radians.
    Amount(x: Angle): Number => x.Radians;
    FromAmount(_: Angle, x: Number): Angle => new Angle(x);

    // SolidAngle <-> a raw amount in steradians.
    Amount(x: SolidAngle): Number => x.Steradians;
    FromAmount(_: SolidAngle, x: Number): SolidAngle => new SolidAngle(x);

    // Length <-> a raw amount in meters.
    Amount(x: Length): Number => x.Meters;
    FromAmount(_: Length, x: Number): Length => new Length(x);

    // Area <-> a raw amount in square meters.
    Amount(x: Area): Number => x.SquareMeters;
    FromAmount(_: Area, x: Number): Area => new Area(x);

    // Volume <-> a raw amount in cubic meters.
    Amount(x: Volume): Number => x.CubicMeters;
    FromAmount(_: Volume, x: Number): Volume => new Volume(x);

    // Speed <-> a raw amount in meters per second.
    Amount(x: Speed): Number => x.MetersPerSecond;
    FromAmount(_: Speed, x: Number): Speed => new Speed(x);

    // Acceleration <-> a raw amount in meters per second squared.
    Amount(x: Acceleration): Number => x.MetersPerSecondSquared;
    FromAmount(_: Acceleration, x: Number): Acceleration => new Acceleration(x);

    // Jerk <-> a raw amount in meters per second cubed.
    Amount(x: Jerk): Number => x.MetersPerSecondCubed;
    FromAmount(_: Jerk, x: Number): Jerk => new Jerk(x);

    // AngularVelocity <-> a raw amount in radians per second.
    Amount(x: AngularVelocity): Number => x.RadiansPerSecond;
    FromAmount(_: AngularVelocity, x: Number): AngularVelocity => new AngularVelocity(x);
```

## Reading this entry

Parameters before the colon are input values; the type after the parameter list is the result.
The first parameter also supplies the dot-call receiver. Type parameters on a declaration are
bare names; free signature variables use `$`. Read the tier and domain guides for units, frames,
invariants, and the difference between a required interface member and a provided body.
